traveler: Simonides of Ceos (Simonides son of Leoprepes)
title: The Half Fee and the Fallen Roof: the Cean Who Sold Praise and Ordered Memory
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Ioulis, Ceos, born to Leoprepes
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The Suda (sigma 439) gives the 56th Olympiad, 556/552 BCE, and adds in the same sentence that some have written the 62nd, 532/528, a variant it neither resolves nor prefers. The conventional 556 is arrived at by counting back from the Parian Marble's death notice of 468/467 at the age of ninety; the Suda itself says eighty-nine, one short. The birthplace, Ioulis on Ceos, is uncontested across the testimonia. The father's name Leoprepes is attested in the patronymic used by Herodotus, by the Parian Marble, and by the epitaph Callimachus quotes.
stops.campa: In the town of Ioulis, above the harbour on the northern flank of Ceos, a son is born to Leoprepes, into a house that knows the price of a chorus and the fee for a song. The island is small and dry, and what it exports is voices: boys trained to sing and step together for the gods, hired out to the festivals of larger places. Antiquity will keep him under his father's name, Simonides son of Leoprepes. On the year of his birth it will not agree, offering two Olympiads a generation apart and no way to choose between them.
suggested_refs: Ioulis (Chora) on Kea, the ancient town site above the north harbour
Suda On Line, entry sigma 439
sources: Suda sigma 439 (Suda On Line, Stoa Consortium)
Marmor Parium A 57 (Parian Chronicle)
D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III: Stesichorus, Ibycus, Simonides and Others (Loeb, 1991), testimonia

stops.name: Karthaia, the chorus drilled above the sea
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, not documented. No contemporary source places Simonides at Karthaia or names him a chorus trainer there; the association is a later inference from his profession and from Ceos's known choral culture, transmitted through the Suda and repeated in modern synthesis (J. H. Molyneux, Simonides: A Historical Study, 1992). The site itself is securely identified and excavated: the temples of Apollo and Athena on the southeastern coast of Kea. The date given here orders the segment only.
stops.campa: On the southeastern coast, in a walled town folded into a ravine that opens to the sea, the temples of Apollo and Athena stand above a terrace wide enough for fifty men to move together. Cean boys are drilled here, for the island's own festivals and for delegations sent abroad. The tradition that Simonides trains them, and is paid to, is the first thing said about his working life. The terrace is stone and the acoustics belong to the ravine, where a chorus master pitches a boy's voice against the sea below.
suggested_refs: The excavated sanctuary and choral terrace at ancient Karthaia, southeastern Kea
sources: Suda sigma 439
J. H. Molyneux, Simonides: A Historical Study (1992)

stops.name: Delos, the Cean delegation before Apollo
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, offered as context rather than as an attested visit. Cean participation in the Delian festival of Apollo is documented in Cycladic epigraphy and in the Delian hymn tradition; no Simonidean text and no ancient testimonium places Simonides himself on Delos. Included because it is the circuit a Cean chorus master works, and flagged as unattested for him personally.
stops.campa: Cean delegations cross to Delos for Apollo's festival, where the islands send their choruses to the god's birthplace and hear each other sing. This is the circuit a chorus master works: a small island's voices measured against Naxos, Paros, Andros, and the crowd of Ionians the hymns describe, in a sanctuary where the prize is not money but the right to be remembered as the best of a season. The practice that formed him is Delian. Nothing in his own surviving verse, and no ancient testimonium, puts him on the island.
suggested_refs: The sanctuary of Apollo on Delos and the Cycladic choral delegations
Callimachus, Hymn to Delos, on the island festival tradition
sources: Cean and Delian cultic epigraphy, general context
D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III (Loeb, 1991)

stops.name: Athens, brought to the city by Hipparchus
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the invitation, reconstructed for the date. Aristotle (or pseudo-Aristotle), Constitution of the Athenians 18, and pseudo-Plato, Hipparchus 228b-c, both say Hipparchus drew Simonides to Athens alongside Anacreon; neither gives a year, and the round age of thirty is a later biographical convenience. The pseudo-Platonic dialogue is not by Plato and is itself a defence of the Peisistratids, so its picture of a cultured Hipparchus is interested testimony.
stops.campa: Hipparchus, son of Peisistratus, spends his family's money on poets, and he sends for two: Anacreon of Teos and Simonides of Ceos. Simonides is about thirty. Athens under the tyrants is building temples, fixing the text of Homer for the Panathenaia, and paying for song at a scale no island can match. The Cean arrives into a court where verse is commissioned like masonry, quantity agreed and price agreed, and he stays exactly as long as the man who commissions it does.
suggested_refs: Pseudo-Plato, Hipparchus 228b-c, on the poets Hipparchus brought to Athens
sources: Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 18
Pseudo-Plato, Hipparchus 228b-c
D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III (Loeb, 1991)

stops.name: Athens, the rivalry with Lasus of Hermione
stops.date_confidence: Tradition. Lasus of Hermione is securely attested at Athens in this period as a dithyrambic poet and musical theorist; the specific rivalry with Simonides comes from later scholiastic and anecdotal material, not from Aristotle's Ath. Pol. 18 or pseudo-Plato's Hipparchus, neither of which mentions Lasus. No contest, year, or chorus is preserved. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Lasus of Hermione is in the same city on the same errand, a dithyrambic poet with theories about music and an appetite for competition. A dithyramb needs fifty men, a trainer, a piper, and a rich citizen to pay for all three; the poet who wins takes the tripod and, more to the point, the next commission. Later tradition remembers the Cean and the Hermionean as rivals working the same buyers and trading tricks. No source names a single contest they both entered.
suggested_refs: Lasus of Hermione, the earliest named theorist of music at Athens
sources: Later scholiastic tradition on Hipparchus' court poets
D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III (Loeb, 1991)

stops.name: Kerameikos, the tyrant killed in the procession
stops.date_confidence: Attested for the killing, inferred for Simonides. Thucydides 6.54-59 and Aristotle, Ath. Pol. 18, both narrate the assassination of Hipparchus by Harmodius and Aristogeiton at the Panathenaia of 514. Thucydides 6.57 puts the killing at the Leokoreion, whose site is disputed between the Kerameikos and the Agora, so the pin is a scholarly choice and not a fixed spot. No source places Simonides in Athens on that day; his presence is the biographers' inference from the patronage ending.
stops.campa: At the Panathenaic procession Harmodius and Aristogeiton kill Hipparchus with knives carried under myrtle, and the patronage that brought Simonides to Athens ends in the street. Hippias rules four more years by terror and then leaves for Persia. The poet appears in no account of the killing and in none of the years after it. What the record shows next is the north: the Thessalian houses, which have money, horses, and no assembly to answer to, and which get him for the following two decades.
suggested_refs: The Leokoreion and the disputed topography of the 514 assassination
The Tyrannicide statues of Harmodius and Aristogeiton, dated by the same Parian Marble entry that records Simonides' chorus victory
sources: Thucydides 6.54-59
Aristotle, Constitution of the Athenians 18
Herodotus 5.55-57

segments.name: Thessaly: The Half Fee and the Fallen Roof

stops.name: Larissa, guest of the Aleuadae
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, plausible but undated. The Aleuadae of Larissa are securely attested as patrons of poets in this period, and the testimonia place Simonides in the Thessalian patronage world of the Aleuadae and the Scopadae; no single Aleuad commission of his survives with a date or a title. The date here orders the segment against the 514 terminus in Athens.
stops.campa: North of the passes, in a plain of horses and wheat, the Aleuadae rule Larissa the way a family rules an estate, and they buy song as they buy horses. Simonides is remembered as their guest, making victory odes and laments for a nobility with no democratic assembly to please and no rival city to impress. Thessalian money pays well and does not argue about subject matter, and a poet with an agreed fee can live here for years without being asked to praise anything but a family. Not one Aleuad commission of his survives with a title or a date on it.
suggested_refs: The Aleuad dynasty of Larissa and their commissions from visiting poets
sources: D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III (Loeb, 1991), testimonia
J. H. Molyneux, Simonides: A Historical Study (1992)

stops.name: Crannon, the song for Scopas and the half fee
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The earliest surviving narrative is Cicero, De Oratore 2.351-352, written in 55 BCE and dramatically set in 91 BCE, roughly four and a half centuries after the supposed event; Cicero marks it himself as report, 'is said to have'. No date within Simonides' life is preserved for it, and no poem of his mentions the episode. The date given here orders the Thessalian segment and is not evidence.
stops.campa: Scopas of the Scopadae gives a banquet at Crannon and commissions an ode for himself. Simonides delivers it, and a long passage of the song praises Castor and Polydeuces, the horse-taming twins, at the host's expense. Scopas counts out half the agreed fee, tells the poet to collect the rest from the Dioscuri since half the poem was theirs, and turns back to his guests. The hall is full and the joke lands well. Simonides takes the half and says nothing, and the room goes on drinking.
suggested_refs: Cicero, De Oratore 2.351-354, the earliest full narrative of the Crannon banquet
sources: Cicero, De Oratore 2.351-352 (attalus.org)
Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 11.2.11-17

stops.name: Crannon, the roof comes down
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction, and disputed in antiquity itself. Cicero, De Oratore 2.353-354, is the earliest full account. Quintilian, Inst. Or. 11.2.11-17, writing about 95 CE, calls the rescue by the two youths 'purely fictitious' on the ground that Simonides nowhere mentions so flattering a miracle, and reports that ancient authorities disagreed over both the victim and the town. The Rhetorica ad Herennium 3.16-24, earlier than Cicero, expounds the loci-and-images method in full and names no inventor and tells no story. Pliny, Natural History 7.24, credits Simonides with the invention and gives no banquet.
stops.campa: A servant comes to say two young men are outside asking for him. Simonides leaves the hall and finds no one at the door. Behind him the roof comes down on the banquet, crushing Scopas and every guest so that the families arriving to claim their dead cannot tell one body from another. Simonides walks the ruin and names them, each by the place at the table where he had seen the man recline. Order of places, order of things: from this hour the mind is furnished like a house, and things are put in rooms to be found again.
stops.quote: the order of places would preserve the order of things, and the symbols of the things would denote the things themselves; so that we should use the places as waxen tablets, and the symbols as letters
stops.quote_source: Cicero, De Oratore 2.354, on the principle Simonides is said to have inferred from the collapse (attalus.org translation)
suggested_refs: Rhetorica ad Herennium 3.16-24, the earliest surviving technical exposition of loci and imagines, which names no inventor
Frances A. Yates, The Art of Memory (1966), chapter 1, which opens on this scene
Joe Grimwade, Memory in Roman Oratory (Cambridge PhD thesis, 2021), which argues for removing Simonides from the literal invention history
sources: Cicero, De Oratore 2.353-354 (attalus.org)
Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 11.2.11-17 (penelope.uchicago.edu)
Pliny the Elder, Natural History 7.24
Marmor Parium A 54, 'ho to mnemonikon heuron'

stops.name: Pharsalus, the other town the story is told of
stops.date_confidence: Variant tradition, mutually exclusive with the preceding stop and left unresolved here. Quintilian, Inst. Or. 11.2.14-15, reports that Apollodorus, Eratosthenes, Euphorion and Eurypylus placed the collapse at Pharsalus, citing Simonides' own verse as authority, while Apollas, Callimachus and Cicero placed it at Crannon; the honoured dead is variously Glaucus of Carystus, Leocrates, Agatharcus or Scopas. Quintilian notes only that Cicero's version 'gained wider circulation'. Both pins are given because antiquity gave both.
stops.campa: Fifty miles south, at Pharsalus, the same disaster is told with different names in it. The man honoured is Glaucus of Carystus, or Leocrates, or Agatharcus, not Scopas; the town is this one, not Crannon; and by one report Simonides' own verse was the authority for it. Apollodorus, Eratosthenes, Euphorion and Eurypylus put the hall here. Apollas, Callimachus and Cicero put it at Crannon. Quintilian, setting the two lists side by side, remarks only that Cicero's version gained wider circulation.
suggested_refs: Quintilian's list of the disagreeing Hellenistic authorities on the banquet story
sources: Quintilian, Institutio Oratoria 11.2.11-17 (penelope.uchicago.edu)

stops.name: Crannon, the ode on how hard it is to be good
stops.date_confidence: Attested as a poem, undated as an event. The song addressed to Scopas is quoted at length in Plato, Protagoras 339a-347a, where it is produced by Protagoras to trap Socrates and only afterwards dissected by Socrates line by line; that dialogue is the reason any of it survives. Neither the year nor the occasion of the original performance is recorded. The pin is the Scopad seat at Crannon and the date orders the segment.
stops.campa: For Scopas, or for the house of Scopas, Simonides writes a song about the difficulty of being good: that a man cannot be made flawless and stay flawless, that circumstance breaks the best of them, and that he will give his praise to anyone who does nothing shameful willingly. It is a nobleman's poem that quietly lowers the standard a nobleman is held to, and the audience is the family paying for it. What survives of it survives because Protagoras recites it in a Platonic dialogue to trap Socrates.
stops.quote: Hardly on the one hand can a man become truly good, built four-square in hands and feet and mind, a work without a flaw.
stops.quote_source: Simonides, ode to Scopas, opening lines, quoted by Protagoras in Plato, Protagoras 339b (Jowett translation)
suggested_refs: Plato, Protagoras 339a-347a, the fullest ancient quotation of any Simonidean lyric
sources: Plato, Protagoras 339a-347a (Jowett tr., classics.mit.edu)
D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III (Loeb, 1991)

segments.name: The War of the Greeks and the Verse for the Dead

stops.name: Marathon, the epigram for the mound
stops.date_confidence: Late and disputed. The competition against Aeschylus for the Marathon epigram is reported only by the anonymous Vita Aeschyli, a Life transmitted with the manuscripts of Aeschylus' plays and centuries later than the events; it is shaped like a literary rivalry topos and cannot establish either the contest or Aeschylus' motive for leaving Athens. The Soros itself is securely identified and excavated. The epigram the competition was fought over does not survive.
stops.campa: The Athenians bury their hundred and ninety-two dead in a mound on the plain and want verses cut over them. A competition is held. Simonides wins it, and Aeschylus, who fought in the battle and whose brother died holding a Persian ship, loses and leaves Athens in anger, or so a Life written long afterward reports. The poet who was not at the battle takes the commission to speak for the men who were. The mound is still on the plain. Not one line of the verse cut over it survives.
suggested_refs: The Soros, the burial mound of the Athenian dead on the plain of Marathon
Vita Aeschyli, the anonymous ancient Life transmitted with the plays
sources: Anonymous Vita Aeschyli
D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III (Loeb, 1991), testimonia

stops.name: Cape Artemisium, the sea fight put into verse
stops.date_confidence: Attested by title only. A poem of Simonides on the sea fight at Artemisium is cited in the ancient testimonia under the title He ep' Artemisioi naumachia; the text does not survive intact, and ancient sources describe its genre inconsistently, some treating it as lyric and some as elegy. The date is the battle's, not the poem's; when it was composed or performed is unknown.
stops.campa: Off the northern cape of Euboea the Greek fleet holds the strait for three days against a Persian navy that has already been mauled by weather, and withdraws when word comes that the pass to the south has fallen. Simonides puts the fighting into verse. Within a month Thermopylae and Salamis will bury the memory of the battle itself. Nothing of the poem survives whole, and the ancients who cite it cannot agree whether a chorus sang it or a single voice recited it.
suggested_refs: The lost Simonidean poem on the sea fight at Artemisium, known by title through the testimonia
sources: D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III (Loeb, 1991), testimonia and titles

stops.name: Thermopylae, the epitaph he pays for himself
stops.date_confidence: Attested, and the single most secure attribution in the whole corpus. Herodotus 7.228 states that of the inscriptions at the pass the Amphictyons set up most, but that the epitaph for the seer Megistias was set up by Simonides son of Leoprepes 'on account of guest-friendship'. Herodotus writes within roughly two generations of the battle. The text quoted here is the Palatine Anthology's version, 7.677.
stops.campa: Megistias the seer of Acarnania reads the sacrifices at the pass, tells the Spartans they will die at dawn, sends his own son away, and stays. Simonides knew him; they had been guests in each other's houses. Of the inscriptions cut at Thermopylae this one is not the Amphictyons' civic work. The poet pays for the stone himself, out of friendship, and puts his friend's name in the first line where a passerby cannot miss it. The pass is a strip of road between the mountain and the sea, wide enough for a cart.
stops.quote: This is the tomb of famous Megistias the prophet, whom the Persians slew after crossing the Spercheius. Though he well knew then the impending fate, he disdained to desert the Spartan leaders.
stops.quote_source: Palatine Anthology 7.677, the epitaph for Megistias, attributed to Simonides and confirmed as his by Herodotus 7.228 (attalus.org translation)
suggested_refs: Herodotus 7.228, the only ancient passage that names Simonides as author of a specific Thermopylae epitaph
sources: Herodotus, Histories 7.228
Palatine Anthology 7.677 (attalus.org)

stops.name: Thermopylae, the couplet for the Spartans
stops.date_confidence: Traditional attribution, not secure. Herodotus 7.228 quotes the couplet and names no author for it, in the same chapter in which he does name Simonides for the Megistias epitaph; the silence is pointed. The assignment to Simonides is later, and modern editors remain cautious. The date orders the segment and is the battle's, not the composition's.
stops.campa: Over the Spartans who held the pass to the last, two lines are cut that do not mourn, do not boast, and do not name the enemy. They are spoken by the dead to a stranger walking past, and they report obedience the way a soldier reports a position held. Antiquity gives the couplet to Simonides. Herodotus, writing it down two generations after the battle and naming Simonides three lines away as the author of another epitaph at this same pass, gives this one to nobody.
stops.quote: Stranger, bear this message to the Spartans, that we lie here obedient to their laws.
stops.quote_source: Palatine Anthology 7.249, the Thermopylae couplet, traditionally attributed to Simonides (attalus.org translation)
suggested_refs: Herodotus 7.228, which quotes the couplet without naming its author
sources: Herodotus, Histories 7.228
Palatine Anthology 7.249 (attalus.org)
D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III (Loeb, 1991)

stops.name: Thermopylae, the epigram that counts
stops.date_confidence: Attributed within the epigram tradition, not securely his. Palatine Anthology 7.248 is transmitted under Simonides' name; the Persian-War epigram corpus circulating under that name is large, and modern scholarship judges only a minority securely his own composition, the rest having been attracted to the most famous name in the genre. No inscription of this text survives on stone.
stops.campa: A third epitaph at the pass simply counts. Four thousand men from the Peloponnese stood here against three million, it says, and the arithmetic is not offered to be checked. It is offered to be carved. Under Simonides' name antiquity assembles a whole body of such verse for the Persian War dead, some of it his and much of it given to him afterward because the name fitted the genre; editors who have gone through it judge only a minority securely his. This one states a number and a place and stops.
stops.quote: Four thousand from Peloponnesus once fought here with three millions.
stops.quote_source: Palatine Anthology 7.248, epitaph for the Peloponnesian dead at Thermopylae, attributed to Simonides (attalus.org translation)
suggested_refs: The Persian-War epigram corpus transmitted under Simonides' name in the Greek Anthology
David Sider, Simonides: Epigrams and Elegies (Oxford, 2021)
sources: Palatine Anthology 7.248 (attalus.org)
David Sider, Simonides: Epigrams and Elegies (OUP, 2021)

stops.name: Salamis, the strait in a single day
stops.date_confidence: Attested by title, text lost. A poem of Simonides on the sea fight at Salamis is cited in the testimonia as He en Salamini naumachia; nothing substantial of it survives and its performance context is unrecoverable. Ancient association of Simonides with the whole 480 commemorative cycle is strong; specific attributions within it vary from source to source.
stops.campa: In the narrows between the island and the Attic shore the Persian fleet is broken in one day, in full view of the Athenians who have abandoned their city and are watching from the beaches. Simonides composes on the battle, for an audience that had seen the thing happen and needed nothing about it described. The poem is named in antiquity and quoted almost not at all. What comes down is a title, He en Salamini naumachia, the sea fight at Salamis, and no text to put under it.
suggested_refs: The lost Simonidean poem on the sea fight at Salamis, known by title through the testimonia
sources: D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III (Loeb, 1991), testimonia and titles

stops.name: Corinth, verses for men buried on Salamis
stops.date_confidence: Attributed, not secured. Palatine Anthology 7.250, for the Corinthian dead at Salamis, is transmitted under Simonides' name; attribution within the epigram corpus is exceptionally unstable and this should be read as reputation rather than certified authorship. The Corinthian dead were buried on Salamis, so the commissioning city and the stone stand in different places; the pin here is the city that paid.
stops.campa: Corinth loses men in the strait and buries them there, on the island, under an epigram. The city commissions it from the poet who has become, in the years after the invasion, the standard voice for this work: a man who never carried a shield, paid to speak in the first person plural for men who did. The phrase he gives them is a razor's edge, Hellas balanced on it, and their lives spent to keep her from going over. The dead stay on Salamis. Only the verse comes home to Corinth.
stops.quote: We lie here, having given our lives to save all Hellas when she stood on a razor's edge.
stops.quote_source: Palatine Anthology 7.250, epitaph for the Corinthian dead at Salamis, attributed to Simonides (attalus.org translation)
suggested_refs: The Corinthian cenotaph tradition on Salamis and its epigram
sources: Palatine Anthology 7.250 (attalus.org)
D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III (Loeb, 1991)

stops.name: Sparta, the dead who do not come home
stops.date_confidence: Reputation rather than documented commission. Epitaphs for Spartan war dead circulate under Simonides' name in the Greek Anthology tradition; many are genuine fifth-century memorial verse, but few can be shown to be his own composition rather than later attraction to his name. No Spartan commission of his is attested by name, date, or magistrate.
stops.campa: Sparta buries its dead where they fall and cuts few words over them. What it wants after the invasion is inscriptions, short ones, for men lying in Boeotia and at the pass and on an island, and the verse that carries those men into the memory of the rest of Greece is circulated afterward under a Cean's name. Did he write them, or did the tradition hand them to the poet it thought of first? Sparta kept no poet of its own, and nothing in the record decides the question.
suggested_refs: The Spartan Persian-War epitaphs in the Greek Anthology, transmitted under Simonides' name
sources: Greek Anthology testimonia
D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III (Loeb, 1991)

stops.name: Kerameikos, the public graves of the Athenians
stops.date_confidence: Attributed, undated. Palatine Anthology 7.253, for the Athenian war dead, is transmitted under Simonides' name. The demosion sema outside the Dipylon gate is securely identified, but no surviving stone carries this text and no source dates the commission. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Outside the Dipylon gate the city lays its war dead in the public ground, tribe by tribe, with a stone, a list of names, and verse cut above the list. The lines given to Simonides for these graves make one argument and repeat it: that dying well is the greater part of excellence, that fortune granted these men that part above others, and that the praise which follows does not grow old. Athens will make the same argument over the same ground for the next hundred years. No stone carrying these particular lines has been found; they come down in the Anthology, under his name.
stops.quote: If to die well be the chief part of virtue, Fortune granted this to us above all others; for striving to endue Hellas with freedom, we lie here possessed of praise that grows not old.
stops.quote_source: Palatine Anthology 7.253, epitaph for the Athenian war dead, attributed to Simonides (attalus.org translation)
suggested_refs: The demosion sema, the Athenian public cemetery outside the Dipylon gate
sources: Palatine Anthology 7.253 (attalus.org)
D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III (Loeb, 1991)

stops.name: Plataea, the elegy that begins at Troy
stops.date_confidence: Attested by direct papyrus discovery, and the strongest surviving evidence for any long Simonidean poem. P.Oxy. LIX 3965, a second-century-CE roll edited by P. J. Parsons and published in 1992, combines with the earlier P.Oxy. 2327 and a quotation in Plutarch to give roughly forty-seven lines of an elegy on the Plataea campaign. The poem's existence and content are secure; its original performance setting, whether a festival for the dead or a Spartan commemoration, is debated and not recoverable.
stops.campa: The last land battle of the invasion is fought under Spartan command on the Boeotian plain, and Simonides writes it as elegy. The poem does not begin at Plataea. It begins at Troy, with Achilles dead and the Greeks sailing home, and it calls on the Muse before it turns to Pausanias and the army standing in the field this summer. The men who fought last month are set in the same measure and the same world as the men who fought for Helen. Who heard it first, and on what occasion, no one can now say.
suggested_refs: P.Oxy. LIX 3965, ed. P. J. Parsons (1992), the 'New Simonides' papyrus
Deborah Boedeker and David Sider, eds., The New Simonides (Oxford, 2001)
sources: P.Oxy. LIX 3965, ed. P. J. Parsons, with P.Oxy. 2327
Boedeker and Sider, eds., The New Simonides (2001)
Plutarch, quoting the elegy

stops.name: Athens, the chorus victory cut into marble
stops.date_confidence: Attested, with one Hellenistic remove. Marmor Parium A 54 records the victory under the archonship of Adeimantos, 477/476 BCE, the same entry that dates the Tyrannicide statues, and names him 'Simonides son of Leoprepes, the Cean, who found the art of memory'. The stone was cut in 264/263 BCE, roughly two centuries after the event. A separate Parian Marble entry gives an Athenian poetic victory in 489/488 to a Simonides often identified as a homonymous grandfather, and the two entries are easily confused.
stops.campa: In the archonship of Adeimantos the city records a choral victory for Simonides son of Leoprepes. The record survives because two centuries later somebody on Paros cuts a chronicle of Greek time into marble and puts this line in it, calling him the Cean and the man who found the art of memory. He has been winning Athenian choruses since Hipparchus paid the bills, through a tyranny, an exile and an invasion, and now under a democracy that has outlasted the men who hired him first. He is close to eighty.
suggested_refs: Marmor Parium A 54, the Parian Chronicle entry for the archonship of Adeimantos
Digital Marmor Parium project
sources: Marmor Parium A 54 (Greek text, Parian Chronicle)
Suda sigma 439, 'He also invented the art of artificial memory'

stops.name: Athens, fifty-seven tripods
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction from a single anonymous epigram. The Greek Anthology preserves an anonymous poem crediting Simonides with fifty-seven dithyrambic victories; no archive, victor list, or inscription can audit the figure, and the epigram's date and author are unknown. The date given here orders the segment.
stops.campa: An epigram counts his tripods: fifty-seven wins in dithyramb. No archive confirms the total, no ancient writer says who counted, and the poem that gives the figure is anonymous and undated. Each win means a chorus of fifty men trained, fed, and costumed at some rich Athenian's expense, and a bronze tripod set up afterward with that citizen's name on it and the poet's somewhere below. They stand along a street of tripods, one monument after another, each of them another man's money and one man's verse.
suggested_refs: The Street of Tripods at Athens, where victorious choregoi set up their monuments
sources: Greek Anthology, anonymous epigram on Simonides' victories
D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III (Loeb, 1991)

stops.name: Olympia, the daughters of storm-footed horses
stops.date_confidence: Fragment genuine, anecdote reported. The line is quoted as Simonides' by Aristotle, Rhetoric 3.2.1405b (PMG 515); the surrounding story of the refused and then accepted commission is Aristotle's report, not independent documentation. No victor, year, or festival is named in the source, and the pin at Olympia is the likeliest setting for a mule-cart victory rather than an attested one.
stops.campa: A man wins the mule-cart race and wants an ode for it. Simonides refuses: he will not write for half-asses. The fee is raised. He writes, and the song opens by hailing the animals as daughters of storm-footed horses, which is true, since a mule's mother is a mare, and which converts the joke of the commission into genealogy. The story is told against him for centuries as proof he would praise anything at the right price. The victor's name is lost. The line is not.
stops.quote: Hail to you, daughters of storm-footed steeds.
stops.quote_source: Simonides, PMG 515, the opening of the mule-cart ode, quoted in Aristotle, Rhetoric 3.2.1405b (classics.mit.edu translation)
suggested_refs: Aristotle, Rhetoric 3.2.1405b, on Simonides and the mule-cart victor
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric 3.2.1405b
D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III (Loeb, 1991), PMG 515

stops.name: Athens, Danae awake in the chest
stops.date_confidence: Text attested, place and date unknown. PMG 543 survives because Dionysius of Halicarnassus quotes it whole in De Compositione Verborum as a specimen of word arrangement; it is the most substantial continuous lyric passage of Simonides to survive. Nothing is recorded of when it was written, where it was performed, or for whom. The Athenian pin and this date order the segment and carry no evidentiary weight.
stops.campa: A woman is shut in a chest with her infant son and pushed out to sea. Simonides writes her awake in the dark: the wind working over the wood, the water coming in at the joints, the child asleep against her with his own untroubled breath. She tells him to sleep. She tells the sea to sleep. She asks forgiveness for the boldness of asking. It is the longest unbroken passage of his lyric anyone still has, and it survives because a critic wanted a specimen of how to arrange words.
suggested_refs: Dionysius of Halicarnassus, De Compositione Verborum, which preserves PMG 543 entire
Orlando Poltera, Simonides lyricus (2008), the standard edition of the lyric fragments
sources: Simonides, PMG 543, quoted in Dionysius of Halicarnassus, De Compositione Verborum
D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III (Loeb, 1991)

stops.name: Athens, painting silent and poetry speaking
stops.date_confidence: Reception, not text. The formulation is attributed to Simonides by Plutarch, De Gloria Atheniensium 346f, writing some five and a half centuries later, and Plutarch gives related versions of it elsewhere in the Moralia; it cannot be treated as a surviving Simonidean sentence. No place or occasion is attached to it in any source. The pin and date order the segment only.
stops.campa: Painting is poetry that keeps quiet; poetry is painting that talks. The sentence travels under his name for two thousand years, through Greek and Latin and every European language that argues about the arts, and no poem of his contains it. It reaches us as a saying, reported five and a half centuries after his death by a writer who gives it in more than one wording, which is what happens to sentences too useful to leave alone. The reporter is Plutarch, in an essay weighing the glory Athens won by arms against the glory it won by art.
stops.quote: Simonides, however, calls painting inarticulate poetry and poetry articulate painting.
stops.quote_source: Plutarch, De Gloria Atheniensium (Moralia) 346f, reporting the saying (Loeb-derived text, penelope.uchicago.edu)
suggested_refs: The ut pictura poesis tradition and its descent from this reported saying
sources: Plutarch, De Gloria Atheniensium 346f
D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III (Loeb, 1991), testimonia

stops.name: Ortygia, received at the tyrant's court
stops.date_confidence: Tradition, broadly accepted, itinerary unrecoverable. The testimonia place Simonides at Hieron's Syracusan court in his last years, in the same patronage world as Pindar and Bacchylides; the anecdotal material is late, the specific dates are not given by any source, and the stories of personal court rivalry between the three poets are late scholiastic inference rather than documented fact. The quote below is from a fourth-century philosophical dialogue and is not a record of speech.
stops.campa: Hieron rules Syracuse from the island of Ortygia and buys the best poetry in the Greek world the way he buys horses and grain. The money has moved to Sicily and the poets have followed it: Pindar of Thebes and Simonides' own kinsman Bacchylides are working the same patron for the same commissions, in a court where an ode can be ordered by the line. The scholars who annotate those odes centuries later will make the competition personal and bitter. Simonides comes west in his eighties.
stops.quote: Would you be pleased to give me information, Hiero, upon certain matters, as to which it is likely you have greater knowledge than myself?
stops.quote_source: Xenophon, Hiero 1 (Dakyns translation, Wikisource), a fourth-century BCE dialogue that stages Simonides questioning the tyrant; not a record of anything he said
suggested_refs: Xenophon, Hiero, the dialogue between the poet and the tyrant
Bacchylides' Syracusan odes for Hieron
sources: Ancient testimonia on Simonides at Hieron's court (Aristotle; Athenaeus)
Scholia to Pindar
Xenophon, Hiero (Dakyns tr., Wikisource)
D. A. Campbell, Greek Lyric III (Loeb, 1991)

stops.name: Ortygia, wealth or wisdom
stops.date_confidence: Attested as an anecdote by Aristotle, Rhetoric 2.16.2 (1391a), who attributes the exchange to Simonides directly; Aristotle writes over a century after Simonides' death and the story is a moral-anecdote genre piece, not a transcript. Neither the occasion nor the year is given, and Hieron's wife is not named. The date orders the segment.
stops.campa: Hieron's wife asks him at table whether it is better to be rich or to be wise. Simonides answers rich, and gives his reason: the wise are to be seen waiting at the doors of the rich. He is a guest in a tyrant's house being invited to flatter philosophy, and he declines to. The answer is repeated for centuries as proof of his greed, and it is also the plainest account anyone has given of how the trade works. Aristotle records it a century and a half later, without a year, without an occasion, and without the woman's name.
suggested_refs: Aristotle, Rhetoric 2.16.2 (1391a), on the wealthy and the wise
sources: Aristotle, Rhetoric 2.16.2 (1391a)

stops.name: Ortygia, the provisions sold
stops.date_confidence: Anecdote reported by Athenaeus in the Deipnosophistae, writing around 200 CE, some six and a half centuries after the event it describes; it illustrates a character type, the shrewd and moderate sage, and is not independent evidence of a transaction. No date or occasion is attached to it.
stops.campa: Hieron keeps him supplied on the scale a tyrant supplies a famous guest: bread, wine, and provision far past what one old man can eat. Simonides sells the surplus. Asked why, he says the arrangement displays two things at once, Hieron's magnificence and his own moderation. Both explanations are exact, and neither is offered as a joke; he is a man who names a price and then keeps his accounts. Athenaeus tells the story six and a half centuries later, as an example of the shrewd and moderate sage.
suggested_refs: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae, on Simonides and Hieron's provisions
Aristophanes, Peace, where his name is already comic shorthand for a poet who works for pay
sources: Athenaeus, Deipnosophistae
Aristophanes, Peace (421 BCE), on Simonides' proverbial love of money

stops.name: Acragas, between Hieron and Theron
stops.date_confidence: Scholiastic tradition, contradicted by silence. The scholia to Pindar credit Simonides with mediating the reconciliation of Hieron of Syracuse and Theron of Acragas. Diodorus Siculus narrates the same reconciliation and does not mention Simonides at all, so the poet's personal diplomatic role is not established. No date, terms, or place of meeting are recorded; the pin is Theron's city.
stops.campa: Theron rules Acragas, Hieron rules Syracuse, they are married into each other's families, and they are close to war. Simonides goes between them. The old Cean has no city behind him, no army, and no stake in Sicily beyond his lodging; what he has is that both men have paid him, and that neither can afford to be the one who insulted the poet. The armies stand down. Diodorus, telling the same reconciliation centuries afterward, does not mention him at all.
suggested_refs: Scholia to Pindar on the reconciliation of Hieron and Theron
Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica, on the same events
sources: Scholia to Pindar
Diodorus Siculus, Bibliotheca Historica

stops.name: Acragas, the end of the ninetieth year
stops.date_confidence: Year attested, place inferred. Marmor Parium A 57 records that the poet Simonides died aged ninety in the archonship of Theagenides at Athens, that is 468/467 BCE; the Suda gives eighty-nine years. Neither source names a place of death. Sicily, and Acragas in particular, is an inference drawn backward from the tomb tradition in Callimachus, not a documented fact. The day, the house, the cause, and the funeral are unknown.
stops.campa: He dies in his ninetieth year, in Sicily, in the archonship of Theagenides at Athens. Nothing records the day, the house, the illness, or who was standing there. He has outlived the tyranny that first hired him, the invasion he made verse for, and every patron who ever paid him, from Hipparchus in the Athenian Agora to Scopas under the roof at Crannon. The chronicle cut on Paros two centuries later gives the year and puts his age at ninety. The Suda gives eighty-nine.
suggested_refs: Marmor Parium A 57, the death notice under the archon Theagenides
sources: Marmor Parium A 57 (Greek text, Parian Chronicle)
Suda sigma 439

stops.name: Acragas, the tomb built and unbuilt
stops.date_confidence: Hellenistic literary tradition, not archaeology. Callimachus, Aetia fr. 64 Harder (= 64 Pfeiffer, 163 Massimilla), stages the poet's ghost complaining that the Acragantines, who had built the tomb in fear of Zeus the god of strangers, allowed a general named Phoenix to pull it down for a defensive tower. No trace of either tomb or tower has been identified. This poem, written some two centuries after the death, is the entire ancient basis for locating the grave at Acragas. The date orders the segment; the demolition is undated.
stops.campa: The people of Acragas bury him outside their walls in fear of Zeus who protects strangers, since a stranger dying among them is the god's business and not theirs. Later a general named Phoenix takes the tomb apart and builds the stones into a tower against a siege. The inscription was still legible when he gave the order. It read: I, the son of Leoprepes, was lying here, the holy man from Ceos. Two centuries afterward a poet in Alexandria gives the ghost a voice to complain of it, and that poem is the whole of the evidence. Neither tomb nor tower has ever been found at Acragas.
stops.quote: I, the son of Leoprepes, was lying here, the holy man from Ceos.
stops.quote_source: The tomb inscription as quoted in Callimachus, Aetia fr. 64 Harder, 'The Tomb of Simonides' (Dickinson College Commentaries)
